title: Vector Algebra — Types, Addition and Scalar Multiplication
topicTitle: Scalar and vector quantities, types of vectors; addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors
notes: **Scalars and vectors.** A scalar has magnitude only (mass, temperature, time); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force). Speed is scalar, velocity is vector.
**Representation.** A vector from A to B is AB = b − a with Cartesian form (x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁); its magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²).
**Equal vectors.** Two vectors are equal when they have the same magnitude AND the same direction; their initial points may differ, so position does not matter.
**Unit vector.** â = a/|a| gives a vector of length 1 along a. The standard basis is i = (1,0,0), j = (0,1,0), k = (0,0,1), and a = xi + yj + zk.
**Zero and negative.** The zero vector 0 has zero magnitude and no definite direction; −a has the same length as a and the opposite direction, with a + (−a) = 0.
**Triangle law.** If a and b are placed head-to-tail, their sum a + b runs from the start of a to the end of b; in components (a₁+b₁, a₂+b₂, a₃+b₃).
**Parallelogram law.** With a and b drawn from a common origin, a + b is the diagonal of the parallelogram they span; this is the same sum as the triangle law.
**Laws of addition.** a + b = b + a (commutative), (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (associative), a + 0 = a, and a + (−a) = 0.
**Scalar multiplication.** k a has magnitude |k|·|a|; it points along a for k > 0, opposite for k < 0, and is the zero vector for k = 0.
**Distributive laws.** k(a + b) = ka + kb and (k + m)a = ka + ma; these make vectors a real vector space, so ordinary algebra applies with care about direction.
**Triangle inequality.** |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality only when a and b point the same way; |a − b| ≥ ||a| − |b|| gives the reverse form.
**Direction ratios and cosines.** For a = (x, y, z), the direction cosines are l = x/|a|, m = y/|a|, n = z/|a|, satisfying l² + m² + n² = 1.
**Exam caution.** Vectors cannot be added to scalars, and |a + b| is not |a| + |b| in general; compute the sum first, then its magnitude.
summary: A vector carries magnitude and direction; equal vectors share both, unit vectors have magnitude one, and the zero vector has none. Vectors add by the triangle or parallelogram law (component-wise), and multiplying by a scalar rescales magnitude, reversing direction when the scalar is negative.
importantStatements: Vector addition is commutative and associative.
For any vector a and scalar k, |k a| = |k| |a|.
The direction cosines of any non-zero vector satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1.
importantNotes: Equal vectors need equal magnitude and direction, not the same starting point.
The zero vector has no direction, so never quote an angle for it.
Unit vectors i, j, k are mutually perpendicular and each has length one.
examShortTricks: Add or subtract vectors component-wise first; draw the triangle only as a visual check.
To get a unit vector quickly, divide each component by the magnitude in one step.
For a point dividing a segment, use the section formula instead of solving simultaneous equations.
formulas: k a = (k a₁, k a₂, k a₃);  |k a| = |k| |a|
examples: Given a = (1, 2, −1) and b = (3, 0, 2), find 2a − b and its magnitude. 2a = (2, 4, −2); 2a − b = (−1, 4, −4); magnitude = √(1 + 16 + 16) = √33.
Find the unit vector along a = (2, −2, 1). |a| = √(4+4+1) = 3, so â = (2/3, −2/3, 1/3) and its direction cosines are exactly those three numbers.
practiceQuestions: If a = (1, −2, 3) and b = (4, 0, −1), compute a + b, 3a − 2b and |a − b|.
Find the direction cosines of the vector joining (1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 3).
Determine k so that (k, 2, 1) is a unit vector.
confusion: Writing |a + b| = |a| + |b|; this holds only when a and b are parallel and point the same way.
Treating a zero component as an undefined direction ratio; it simply means the direction cosine in that axis is zero.
practice: Draw the parallelogram for two chosen vectors and verify the diagonal equals their component-wise sum.
Verify the distributive law k(a + b) = ka + kb numerically for k = −2.
universalFacts: The set of all 3-D real vectors with these two operations is a vector space over ℝ.
Any vector can be written uniquely as a linear combination of i, j and k.
specialNotes: Position vectors are measured from the origin; displacement vectors are differences of position vectors.
A negative scalar multiple reverses direction, which is why braking is a negative acceleration vector.
examNotes: Give both magnitude and direction when a question asks for a vector quantity.
Show component-wise working; examiners award marks for each correct component.
